lesson.title: Probe Compensation: Tuning the Divider for Every Frequency
lesson.summary: Because stray capacitance in the scope and probe distorts a 10x probe's resistive divider at higher frequencies, every 10x probe includes an adjustable trimmer capacitor that must be tuned, while watching a calibration square wave, so its edges appear flat and sharp rather than rounded or overshooting.
lesson.body:
The 9 megaohm to 1 megaohm resistive divider inside a 10x probe gives exactly a 10:1 ratio for a steady, unchanging DC voltage. But real signals change over time, and change quickly for fast edges and high frequencies, and at those higher frequencies, small amounts of stray capacitance, from the probe's cable and from the scope's input circuitry itself, start to matter. You already know from working with capacitors that a capacitor's opposition to changing voltage depends on frequency, so this parasitic capacitance effectively adds a second, frequency dependent divider on top of the resistive one, and that second divider does not automatically match the clean 10:1 resistive ratio.

To correct for this, every 10x probe includes a small adjustable trimmer capacitor, usually accessible through a tiny screw or dial near the probe's connector, wired in parallel with the 9 megaohm resistor. Adjusting this capacitor forms a matching capacitive divider that, when tuned correctly, keeps the overall 10:1 ratio accurate across a wide range of frequencies, not just at DC. This process, adjusting that trimmer until the divider is balanced at every frequency, is called probe compensation, and it needs to be checked whenever you use a probe on a different scope, or periodically on the same one, because the exact match depends on the specific input capacitance of whichever scope channel the probe is plugged into.

You compensate a probe by connecting it to a known reference signal, most oscilloscopes provide a calibration output for exactly this purpose, typically a low voltage square wave around 1 kHz, and watching the displayed shape while you turn the trimmer. A square wave is ideal for this because its sharp vertical edges make any distortion in the divider immediately visible. If the trimmer capacitance is too low, the probe is undercompensated, and the top of each pulse appears rounded or sloped rather than flat, as if the edges were being softly filtered. If the trimmer capacitance is too high, the probe is overcompensated, and you instead see overshoot, a spike above the flat level right after each edge, sometimes followed by a bit of ringing before it settles. Turn the trimmer while watching the screen until neither effect is visible and the top of each pulse is flat with sharp corners; that is a correctly compensated probe, and only once it is compensated should you trust it for accurate voltage or timing measurements, particularly on fast edges or high frequency signals.
